difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY — read four bar heights and take a weighted mean of a linear function (one concept, single-step computation); about a minute.
stem:
The number of patients per shift ($X$) consulting Dr. Gita in her past 100 shifts is shown in the figure. If the amount she earns is ₹ $1000(X - 0.2)$, what is the average amount (in ₹) she has earned per shift in the past 100 shifts?

Note: The figure shown is representative.

![Figure: Bar chart of the number of shifts (vertical axis, 0 to 50) against the number of patients per shift X (horizontal axis). X = 5 in 20 shifts, X = 6 in 40 shifts, X = 7 in 30 shifts and X = 8 in 10 shifts; each bar is labelled with its value.](/pyq/2025/fig/Q10-1.png)

solution.quick: From the chart, the mean number of patients per shift is $\dfrac{5(20) + 6(40) + 7(30) + 8(10)}{100} = 6.3$. Earnings are linear in $X$, so the average earning is $1000(6.3 - 0.2) = 6100$, i.e. ₹6,100 — option **(A)**.

steps.title: Read the frequency distribution from the chart
steps.body:
| Patients per shift $X$ | Number of shifts $f$ |
|---|---|
| 5 | 20 |
| 6 | 40 |
| 7 | 30 |
| 8 | 10 |
| **Total** | **100** |

The frequencies add up to 100, matching ‘past 100 shifts’.

steps.title: Mean number of patients per shift
Same result by linearity
steps.body:
The average of a linear function equals the function of the average:

$$\overline{1000(X - 0.2)} = 1000(\bar X - 0.2) = 1000(6.3 - 0.2) = 1000 \times 6.1 = 6100.$$

Answer: **(A) 6,100**.

solution.teaching:
**Mean of a frequency distribution.** When a value $x_i$ occurs $f_i$ times, the mean is the *weighted* average

$$\bar x = \frac{\sum_i f_i x_i}{\sum_i f_i}.$$

Each value counts as many times as it occurs. Simply averaging the distinct values (5, 6, 7, 8 → 6.5) ignores how often each occurs and is wrong unless all frequencies are equal.

**Linearity of the mean.** If every observation is transformed by $y = a x + b$, then

$$\bar y = \frac{\sum f_i (a x_i + b)}{\sum f_i} = a\,\frac{\sum f_i x_i}{\sum f_i} + b\,\frac{\sum f_i}{\sum f_i} = a\bar x + b.$$

So you never need to compute the earning shift by shift: find $\bar X$ once and plug it into the formula. (In probability language this is $E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b$.) The rule works only for *linear* transformations; for something like $X^2$, the mean of the squares is not the square of the mean.

In this question, $a = 1000$ and $b = -200$: every consultation earns ₹1,000, and ₹200 is deducted per shift. With $\bar X = 6.3$, the average earning is $1000(6.3) - 200 = 6100$.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Weighted mean $\bar X = 630/100 = 6.3$, and by linearity the average earning is $1000(6.3 - 0.2) = 6100$.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: $6{,}300 = 1000 \times 6.3$: it forgets the $-0.2$ term, i.e. the ₹200 deducted in every shift.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: $6{,}000 = 1000 \times 6$: it uses the most frequent value $X = 6$ (the mode, also the median) instead of the mean and drops the $-0.2$; the actual average is 6,100.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: $6{,}500 = 1000 \times 6.5$, where $6.5$ is the unweighted average of 5, 6, 7, 8: it ignores both the shift frequencies and the $-0.2$ term.

solution.shortcut: Mean of a linear function = the function of the mean: $\bar X = 6.3$, so the average earning is $1000(6.3 - 0.2) = 6100$.
solution.commonTrap: Forgetting the $-0.2$ in $1000(X - 0.2)$ and choosing 6,300, or averaging 5, 6, 7, 8 without weighting by the number of shifts.

The second official image (Q10-2) shows only the next section heading ('Q. 11 – Q. 35 carry one mark each.') and contains no part of this question.

answerVerification.checkCode:
freq={5:20,6:40,7:30,8:10}; n=sum(freq.values())
meanX=sum(x*f for x,f in freq.items())/n
avg=sum(1000*(x-0.2)*f for x,f in freq.items())/n
print(n, meanX, avg, 1000*(meanX-0.2))
answerVerification.notes: Independent solve (weighted mean $\bar X = 6.3$; average earning $1000(6.3 - 0.2) = 6100$) gives (A), agreeing with the official key A. The Python check computes the weighted mean from the chart frequencies and the average earning both directly and via linearity.
